ROPE ABOUT HIS NECK. The Wrong Negro Narrowly Escapes Being Lynched.
Mhoon's Landing, Miss., Aug. 29.—Charley Wilson, a negro from Greenville, Miss., came within an inch of paying with his life for the murder of Tom Mike, a levee contractor. He was caught by a band of men who were searching for Dick Johnson, the murderer, near Mhoon's Landing, and his resemblance to Johnson was so close that a rope had been swung over the limb of a tree, the noose was around his neck, ten determined men had hold of the rope preparatory to swinging the negro into eternity when the discovery was made that this man had a scar on his face which was absent from the face of the murderer. The hands of the lynchers were stayed, and further investigations showed that he was an innocent man.

Joplin, Mo., Aug 26. — Walter Ayers, a saloon loafing negro, drank a pint of whisky last night and died from the effects three hours afterward. The United States Wants to Know the Powers' Intentions.
A special all-day cabinet meeting on the Chinese question was held August 29. It is understood that the cabinet completed preparations of a plan for clearing away much of the uncertainty that now exists as to the future in China and outlined its views in writing. What is sought is an agreement among the powers for terminating the indefinite status of affairs in China. It is believed that the point has been reached where it is proper that there should be a clear expression of purpose on the part of the principal powers, in order that the United States government may know how far it may go consistently in the execution of the common programme.

NEGRO BOY LYNCHED. He Had Committed Robbery and Arson and Had Confessed His Crime. NEW ORLEANS, La., Aug. 23.—A negro boy, Irvin Love, was lynched at Norfield, Lincoln county, Miss., last night. Two weeks ago, the house of Joe Sassero, at Norfield, was robbed and set on fire and burned to the ground, the family barely escaping with their lives. Love was suspected. He was arrested and taken to Norfield when he confessed his guilt and returned most of the stolen property. While the officers were conveying Love to the county jail, they were overpowered by a mob, the negro taken from them and hanged to a tree by the roadside.

A few days later certain circumstances pointed to Irvin Love, a young negro about 20 or 21, as the guilty party. Love disappeared, after having been seen in Bogue Chitto offering to trade a pistol which was afterward identified as one Mr. Sasser had left in his house. Last week he was located at Fernwood, where he had gone to work for the Enochs Lumber Co., and Mr. R. L. Brent, of Bogue Chitto, went down and effected his arrest and brought him back.

On being arraigned before Justice R. R. Albritton, of Beat 4, last Wednesday on the charges of burglary, theft and arson, it is stated he plead guilty and made a full confession. In his confession, he declared that the burning of the house was an afterthought and not originally intended. He noticed Mr. Sasser and family leave home, he said, the Sunday the dwelling was burnt, and then slipped into the house for the purpose of committing robbery. He took a revolver, a razor and a bottle of whisky, and was about to leave, when he noticed some fat lightwood lying on the hearth; whereupon the thought occurred to him that if he would use this and set fire to the house, the theft would not be discovered—a thought that was promptly carried into execution. He gave away a part of the whisky afterward to some friends, and offered to trade the pistol in Bogue Chitto, as above stated, and this led to his pursuit and capture.

On pleading guilty, Love was committed to jail in default of bond. By this time the news of his capture and confession had spread and there was no little suppressed excitement and indignation among the people living in the locality of his crime. Justice Albritton, fearing he might be foully dealt with, if he started him to Brookhaven in charge of Acting Constable Moak, locked the prisoner in a back room of his residence and directed the Constable to telephone to Sheriff Applewhite to come down and escort him to jail, as he feared violence. THE LEADER learns from Sheriff Applewhite that he received this message between 3 and 4 o'clock Wednesday afternoon, and promptly took the cannon ball train here at 4:10 for Norfield, where the train made a special stop to allow him to get off. The Sheriff says he was met at the Norfield depot by a young man who informed him that the negro had already been taken by a mob "from Justice Albritton's back gallery," and that he was too late. However, he lost no time getting in a buggy with Mr. Hodges, who was awaiting him, and proceeded at once to go to Justice Albritton's. After passing Mt. Pleasant Church, and when in about a half mile or three-quarters of the Justice's, he was met by a stranger, claiming to be a messenger from Albritton, who informed him that the negro was to be taken and hanged by the mob at a point near Brister's dummy line on the Bogue Chitto road, where a negro had been hung some five or six years ago. On turning about and proceeding to this point, the Sheriff found the pretended messenger from Justice Albritton and two others had already preceded him and were apparently awaiting the approach of the mob. Subsequent developments showed that a very clever ruse had been played on Sheriff Applewhite, and that the mob did not really get possession of the prisoner until about the time the Sheriff got back to Norfield from his trip up the Bogue Chitto road. Justice Albritton had indiscreetly made public the fact that he had sent for the Sheriff and expected him down that evening, and therefore friends of the mob were on the alert to mislead him in the way outlined above.

Next morning the negro was found suspended to a gum tree, with a piece of $ \frac{5}{8} $ inch grass rope, on the Summit road, a few hundred yards south of the Mt. Pleasant Church. Sheriff Applewhite proceeded to the spot, with Circuit Clerk Oliver, Acting Coroner, and after a jury was empaneled and as full an investigation had as practicable, a verdict was returned that the deceased had come to his death at the hands of parties to the jury unknown.

james-wilson-chicago-1900-08.A1:
A Narrow Escape.
Chicago, Aug. 24—James Wilson, a negro ventriloquist, had a narrow escape from lynching in this city last night at the hands of a crowd which mistook him for a kidnapper. In his efforts to attract an audience, Wilson stood on a street corner, caressing what appeared to be a white infant, but what was really a rag baby. He then "threw his voice" into the rag baby and a woman leaped toward him. He ran and a crowd pursued shouting "Kill him, Lynch him; he is a kidnapper". The crowd had almost overtaken the fleeing negro when he jumped on a street car and the conductor aided him in keeping the crowd back.

james-wilson-chicago-1900-08.A3:
Mob Thought Negro Was Beating White Baby.
REPUBLIC SPECIAL

REPUBLIC SPECIAL

Chicago, Ill., Aug. 24.—James Wilson, a negro ventilolquist, took his rag baby to the corner of Noble and Blackhawk streets last night and expected to have a little quiet fun with the populace. He had it, and he still lives, for which fact he has a pair of long, speedy legs to thank.

Anxious to attract an audience, he began shaking the "baby" viciously, whereat the ink-faced child began to wail piteously. The shades of night caused a nearsighted woman to believe that the negro was maitreating a white child.

"He's a kidnaper," she cried, whereupon half a hundred angry citizens made a dash toward Wilson. It looked for a few moments as if there would be another negro riot. He adjourned the show and started to break all sprinting records in North Ashland avenue. The crowd was close at his heels, but he managed to board a street car. The conductor came to his rescue, and by vigorously flourishing a controlling lever, kept the crowd off the car. Wilson threw his rag baby at his pursuers and sat down to get his wind.

WHY DRIED LIZARD IS HIGH.

If It Were Not Medicinal the Tariff Act Would Be More Lenient.

Some time ago, in looking over the market for Chinese edibles and delicacies, the enterprising firm of Bow Tsue Tong & Co., importers, of San Francisco, discovered a shortage in the supply of dried lizards and imported a quantity. The Custom-house Appraiser looked through the Dingley act to see what the tariff on dried lizards was, but the framers of this law had forgotten to mention this commodity. The Appraiser learned that the usual way of utilizing the lizard after he had been properly dried was to simmer him on a stove, making a tea similar to the herb tea so justly popular in rural districts. Then the patient sipped the concoction. Now just where lizard tea ceases to be an extract of meat and becomes a medicinal preparation the Board of Appraisers does not attempt to say, but of this much it is sure, that it is a medicinal preparation and should pay 25 per cent ad valorem. The Collector at San Francisco was sustained in fixing this rate instead of the 10 per cent the importers claimed as proper on "unmanufactured" articles. How Tsue Tong & Co. attempted to show that dried lizards were on all fours with horned frogs, the treasury having ruled in the case of the frog that it was an article of food. The Board of Appraisers, however held that the question of the medicinal value of the frog was never considered, and so the case was different.

Rev. T. C. Schilling Resigns at the Close of the Meeting.
The annual protracted meeting was commenced at Liberty Baptist church on last Saturday by Elder T. C. Schilling and conducted by him from day to day until Wednesday when it closed. The attendance was large and the audience attentive to the exercises throughout Mr. Schilling has been the pastor of this church for the past five years, and under his ministrations the church has prospered in its Christian work as well as in many accessions to the membership, among whom with few exceptions harmony and brotherly love prevail.

It is to be regretted that this is his last protracted service with the Liberty Baptist church, as he has declined another call to the pastorate charge of this church, where he has so long and acceptably labored, and where he has accomplished so much for the cause of Christ and the good of the church, and where all were interested and agreeably entertained by his services. When he leaves here for other fields of labor he will carry with him the kindest wishes, not only of the church, but of the community to whom he so faithfully preached.

He will long be remembered by this community for his good works done at this place and which will follow; the good result of which will be seen and felt in the distant future.

After the close of the meeting conference was called, and the church elected, as the successor of Elder Schilling, Elder J. H. Lane to the pastorate of the church for the next year at the same salary paid to Elder Schilling.
